statement: Let \(n \geq 3\) be a positive integer. Consider an \(n \times n\) board. In each step, the colors of the 5 squares that make up a P-pentomino (as shown in the figure, which can be rotated by \(90^\circ\), \(180^\circ\), or \(270^\circ\)) all change color: black squares become white and white squares become black. Initially all squares are white. Determine for which values of \(n\) it is possible, through a series of steps, to make all squares on the board black.
figure_description: A P-pentomino: a 2×3 rectangle of 6 squares with one corner square removed, forming a shape of 5 squares. The figure can be rotated by 90°, 180°, or 270°.

statement: Find all positive integers \(n\) such that all prime factors of \(2^n - 1\) are less than or equal to 7.

Let \(ABC\) be a triangle and \(M\) the midpoint of \(BC\). Let \(\Omega\) be the circumscribed circle such that \(A, B, C \in \Omega\). Let \(P\) be the intersection of \(\Omega\) and \(AM\). Let \(AF\) be an altitude of the triangle with \(F \in BC\), and \(H\) the orthocenter. Let \(K\) and \(T\) be the intersections of \(MH\) and \(PF\) with \(\Omega\), respectively. Demonstrate that the circumscribed circle of triangle \(KTF\) is tangent to \(BC\).

A positive integer is called good if it equals the difference of two positive perfect cubes. For example, 7 is a good prime because \(2^3 - 1^3 = 7\). Determine all possible last digits of a good prime. Give all possibilities.

Let \(n\) be a positive integer. Beto writes a list of \(n\) non-negative integers on a board. He then performs a move (two steps) of the following type: First, for each \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, n\), he counts how many numbers on the board are less than or equal to \(i\); let \(a_i\) be this count. Next, he erases all numbers from the board and writes \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\).

For example, if \(n = 5\) and the initial numbers are \(0, 7, 2, 6, 2\), after the first move the board will show \(1, 3, 3, 3, 3\); after the second move they will be \(1, 1, 5, 5, 5\), and so on.

a) Show that, for every \(n\) and every initial configuration, there will come a time after which the numbers will no longer be modified by this move.

b) Find (as a function of \(n\)) the minimum value of \(k\) such that, for any initial configuration, the moves from move number \(k\) onward will not change the numbers on the board.

There is a ping pong tournament with \(n \geq 3\) participants numbered \(1, 2, \ldots, n\). At the start, all players form a line ordered from 1 to \(n\). Players 1 and 2 play the first match. The winner goes to the front of the line and the loser is placed behind the last person in line. In the next play, the first two players in line face each other; the winner goes to the front and the loser to the end, and so on. After \(N\) matches, the tournament ends. Player number 1 won \(a_1\) matches, player number 2 won \(a_2\) matches, and so on until player \(n\), who won \(a_n\) matches (so \(a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n = N\)). Determine how many games each player has lost, based on \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\).
